opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so in principle you could do that. You could say, "I have a value function, I'll evaluate every legal next board, and then softmax over those values to get a distribution over moves." And for a small action space that's not crazy. But a few things make an explicit policy head much nicer in practice.

The first is just compute. In Go you've got up to around 361 legal moves at each position. If your policy comes from normalizing values, then to get a prior over moves at a single node you need to run the value network on every one of those child positions. That's hundreds of forward passes just to decide where to look. With a policy head, one forward pass on the current board gives you a full distribution over all moves at once. And since MCTS is basically a machine for deciding where to spend your limited simulation budget, a cheap prior is a big deal.

The second is that they're learning subtly different things, and the policy is often the easier target. The value is asking, "Who wins from here?", which is a very noisy, global, long-horizon question. The policy is asking, "What would a strong player do here?", and that's often a more local, pattern-like judgment. A lot of good moves are recognizable from shape before you can say precisely how much they change your win probability. So the policy can be sharp and useful even when the value estimates for the children are all clustered around 0.5 and basically indistinguishable after you normalize.

That ties into a third point, which is calibration. If you softmax values, the shape of your prior depends heavily on a temperature you have to pick, and small errors in the value net get amplified or flattened in weird ways. In AlphaZero-style training, the policy target is the visit count distribution from search, so the policy is directly trained to predict where search ends up spending its effort. That's exactly the quantity you want as a prior in PUCT. It's self-consistent in a way that a normalized value isn't.

And then finally, it gives you a nice division of labor. The policy narrows the breadth of the search, telling you which few moves are worth considering, and the value cuts off the depth, so you don't have to roll out to the end of the game. You get two complementary signals rather than one signal used twice. And the search acts as a policy improvement operator: you take the network's prior, run search, get a better distribution, and distill that back into the policy. That loop is a lot cleaner when the policy is its own explicit object.

r001.rationale: The response describes a feedback loop in which the policy prior guides search, search produces an improved move distribution, and that distribution is distilled back into the policy; it says this loop is cleaner with an explicit policy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I get a lot, because on the surface it seems redundant. If you have a value function that's good, you could just look at every legal move, evaluate the resulting board, softmax over those values, and call that your policy. Why learn a separate head?

The first reason is just compute. In something like Go you have a few hundred legal moves at the root, and if you want to derive a prior from values you have to actually expand every child and run the value network on each one before you can even decide where to spend your search budget. A policy head gives you that distribution in a single forward pass of the parent. That's a couple hundred evaluations versus one, and MCTS is all about where you spend your evaluations.

The second reason is more subtle, and it's about what the two functions are actually estimating. The value of a next board is an estimate of outcome under optimal play from that position. The policy is an estimate of what a strong player would do from this position, and those are not the same thing, especially when the value function is imperfect. Value estimates for sibling boards are noisy, and the differences between them are often tiny. If you normalize over those, a little bit of error gets amplified into a very confident, very wrong prior. The policy is trained directly on the visit distribution from search, which is a much smoother, more robust target. It's effectively distilling the result of thousands of rollouts into a single prediction, so it already encodes a lot of lookahead that a one-step value comparison doesn't.

And then there's a bootstrapping argument. The policy acts as the prior in the PUCT formula, the value acts as the leaf evaluation, and the search improves on both of them. That's the whole policy iteration loop in AlphaZero. Search is the policy improvement operator, and the network learns to imitate the improved policy. If you derived the policy from the values, you'd be collapsing that into one estimator, and you lose the ability for the search to correct one with the other. In practice they catch each other's mistakes.

The last thing I'd say is that in robotics, which is where I spend most of my time, this matters even more, because the action space is continuous and you can't enumerate next states at all. You need something that proposes actions, and that's a policy by definition. So I think of the explicit policy as the thing that generalizes beyond board games, and the normalized-value trick as a special case that only works when branching is small and your value function is already really good.

r001.rationale: The response describes an AlphaZero policy-iteration loop: search improves the policy, the network learns to imitate that improved policy, and the policy and value estimates can correct each other.

astra-6.text:
The value function and the policy are answering different questions. The value function says, “How good is this position?” The policy says, “Which moves are worth considering?” You can derive a policy from values, but you have to evaluate all the possible next positions first. If the branching factor is large, that’s expensive.

An explicit policy gives you a prior over moves in one forward pass, so you can spend your search budget on the promising ones. And you can train it on the results of search. You do this expensive computation, discover a better distribution over moves, and then distill that back into the policy. The next time you encounter a similar position, you have some of that computation available without having to repeat the whole search.

Also, normalizing values doesn’t necessarily give you a useful distribution over actions. A move’s probability of winning isn’t the probability with which you should choose that move. If one move wins with probability 0.9 and another with probability 0.8, normalizing those numbers gives you almost a coin flip. You can introduce a temperature or some other transformation, but that’s an additional decision rule. An explicit policy learns that allocation of attention directly.

r001.rationale: The response says search discovers a better move distribution, which is distilled back into the explicit policy and reused in similar positions. This describes improving the policy through feedback from search.

sol-6.1.text:
The policy and the value function are answering different questions. The value function asks, “How good is this position if I play well from here?” The policy asks, “Which moves are worth considering?” And that second question is really useful when you have a limited search budget.

Suppose there’s one good move and a hundred bad moves. With a policy, you can put most of your search into the promising move immediately. If you’re deriving that distribution from successor-state values, you have to evaluate all those successor states first. And simply normalizing the values doesn’t necessarily give you a useful distribution over actions. Two moves might both lead to a win under optimal play, but one requires finding a very narrow sequence, while the other is much easier to execute.

So I like having a policy explicitly represent where to spend computation. Search can improve that policy, and then you train the policy to imitate what search discovered. The value function helps you evaluate the branches; the policy helps you decide which branches to explore.

r001.rationale: The response says search improves the policy and the policy is then trained to imitate what search discovered, describing a feedback loop as a reason to model the policy explicitly.
